q: Oro, Ambra and Rubino on a Marsala label record what?
exp: Gold, amber and ruby. Sweetness is declared separately as secco, semisecco or dolce on the Fine and Superiore tiers, while Vergine takes no sweetening and is dry by definition; ageing runs Fine, Superiore, Superiore Riserva, then Vergine.

q: Spirit goes in partway through fermentation and nothing sweet is ever added. Which French category does that describe?
exp: The sweetness is grape sugar the yeast never reached, exactly as in Port. Most sit between fifteen and eighteen percent alcohol. A vin de liqueur differs in that the spirit goes into unfermented must.

q: Which southern Rhone village is as well known for a sweet fortified Muscat as for its red wine?
exp: Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise is made from Muscat Blanc a Petits Grains, grapey and scented with orange blossom, and it is traditionally poured with melon or a fruit tart.

q: Banyuls and Maury build their sweet fortified reds on which variety?
exp: Aged in a deliberately oxidative style, they take on coffee, walnut and dried fig. Banyuls is one of the few wines that can stand up to dark chocolate.

q: Casks left deliberately part full, in the sun or in a warm loft, develop which prized character?
exp: Rancio is a controlled oxidative note of walnut, coffee and old wood. The same word describes the equivalent character in very old Sherry and in Armagnac.

q: One fungus can either destroy a crop or make a great sweet wine. What decides which?
opts: Whether dry weather follows the damp
Whether the grapes are red or white
Whether the vines are young or old
exp: Damp mornings let Botrytis cinerea establish itself, but if the wet keeps up it turns to grey rot and the fruit is lost. Dry, breezy afternoons are what turn infection into concentration.

q: Which meeting of rivers supplies the autumn mists that make Sauternes possible?
opts: The Vienne running into the Loire
The cold Ciron running into the warmer Garonne
The Dordogne running into the Gironde
The Saone running into the Rhone
exp: The Ciron leaves a shaded forest cold and chills the surface of the Garonne, so fog forms at night and burns off by midday. That daily rhythm is the reason the appellation exists where it does.

q: Pickers go through a Sauternes vineyard several times in one harvest. Why?
opts: Only the shrivelled berries are taken each pass
The grapes have to be sorted by colour on the vine
The pickers are paid by the day rather than the crate
Each pass gathers a different grape variety
exp: Noble rot spreads through a vineyard unevenly, so each pass takes only what has shrivelled. Those passes are the tries, and there can be half a dozen across several weeks. Yields fall to a fraction of a dry white's, which is most of why the wine costs what it does.

q: Which German Pradikat level calls for individually selected, shrivelled botrytised berries?
exp: Beerenauslese sits just below it and Eiswein alongside. All of them depend on the season, so they are made only in favourable years and in tiny quantities.

q: A Hungarian label gives a number of puttonyos. What does that number record?
opts: The years the wine spent in cask
The number of grape varieties blended
The sweetness of a Tokaji Aszu
exp: It began as a count of hods of botrytised aszu berries kneaded into a base wine, and now stands for a minimum residual sugar. Five and six puttonyos are the usual bottlings.

q: Coteaux du Layon, Bonnezeaux and Quarts de Chaume concentrate which grape?
exp: Chenin's searching acidity carries great sweetness without turning cloying, and the Layon valley draws noble rot in the best years. Vouvray makes sweet wine from the same grape further upstream.

q: Fruit has to be picked and pressed while still frozen solid for which style?
exp: Water in the berry stays behind as ice in the press, so only concentrated sugar and acid run off. Germany's Eiswein and Canada's icewine are the same idea under two names.

q: Which hardy hybrid does most of the work in Canadian icewine?
exp: Vidal has thick skins that survive months hanging into winter without splitting. Riesling and Cabernet Franc are also used, in far smaller quantities.

q: Bunches are laid on racks in an airy loft for months, losing water and gaining concentration. Which Italian practice is that?
exp: Valpolicella dries Corvina and its partners this way over the winter. Fermented out the result is Amarone; stopped while still sweet it is Recioto.

q: Amarone and Recioto della Valpolicella begin from the same dried grapes. What separates them?
opts: Amarone ends dry and Recioto is sweet
Recioto is fortified and Amarone is not
Recioto is white and Amarone is red
Amarone is dried and Recioto is not
exp: Amarone is fermented right out, and its name means bitter. Recioto is stopped with sugar still in it, is the older of the two, and was the region's original sweet speciality.

q: Dried on mats, fermented in small sealed barrels under the roof and poured with cantucci: which Tuscan wine?
exp: Trebbiano and Malvasia dry for months, then spend years in caratelli sealed with a madre left from an earlier batch. The results run from unctuous to nearly dry.
